chunks: Saad ibn Abdullah said: Narrated to me a group of scholars including Abu Hashim Dawood ibn al-Qasim al-Ja'fari, and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Abbasi, and Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah, and Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Amari, and others who were imprisoned because of the killing of Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Abbasi.

That Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his brother Ja'far entered upon them at night. They said: One night we were sitting and talking when we heard the movement of the prison door, which alarmed us. Abu Hashim was unwell, so he said to one of us: Look and see what you see. He looked towards the door and saw that the door was open, and two men had been brought into the prison, and the door was closed and locked. He went up to them and said: Who are you? One of them said: We are a group from the Talibiyyin, we have been imprisoned. He asked: Who are you? He replied: I am al-Hasan ibn Ali, and this is Ja'far ibn Ali. He said to them: May I be your ransom, if you see fit, come to the house. They hurried to us and to Abu Hashim and informed us, and they entered. When Abu Hashim saw them, he rose from the rug that was beneath him, kissed the face of Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him), and seated him on it, and Ja'far sat near him. Ja'far called out: 'Washtana!' in a loud voice, meaning his slave girl. Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) rebuked him and said to him: Be silent. And they saw in him the signs of intoxication, and sleep overcame him while he was sitting with them, so he slept in that state. And what is narrated about him and from him of shameful actions and sayings is more than can be counted, we will keep our book free from that.

key_terms.جَعْفَرُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ: Ja'far ibn Ali (brother of the Imam)
key_terms.وَاشْطَنَاهُ: Washtana (calling out to a slave girl)

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Imam Hasan al-Askari's imprisonment with Abu Hashim Dawud?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Ghayba highlights the historical reality of Imam Hasan al-Askari's (a.s.) imprisonment alongside his brother Ja'far, illustrating the 'Shu'ubiyyah' or 'Veridical' view by depicting their human experiences, such as intoxication and familial interactions. It serves as a key narrative in Shia scholarship to balance the doctrine of infallibility (Ismah) with the Imams' tangible presence in history, showing that their humanity did not detract from their spiritual status.
